why.correct: Carbohydrate: 45 g × 4 = 180 kcal. Protein: 10 g × 4 = 40 kcal. Fat: 5 g × 9 = 45 kcal. Total: 180 + 40 + 45 = 265 kcal.
options: 220 kcal leaves out the fat. Its 5 g still supply 5 × 9 = 45 kcal.
240 kcal counts the fat at 4 kcal per gram, like carbohydrate. Fat supplies about 9 kcal per gram.
Correct. 180 + 40 + 45 = 265 kcal.
540 kcal counts all 60 g at 9 kcal per gram. Only fat supplies 9; carbohydrate and protein supply about 4.

why.correct: Energy from fat = 10 g × 9 kcal/g = 90 kcal. Share = 90 ÷ 200 = 0.45, or 45%.
options: Correct. 90 kcal of the 200 come from fat.
5% is grams of fat divided by kilocalories (10 ÷ 200). Convert the fat to kilocalories first.
20% counts fat at 4 kcal per gram (40 ÷ 200). Fat supplies about 9 kcal per gram.
90 is the kilocalories from fat, not the percentage. Divide by the bar's 200 kcal.

why.correct: Vitamin C keeps the iron in the collagen-strengthening enzymes in its working form. Without it, new collagen is weak, so small vessels break (bruises, bleeding gums) and wounds cannot build strong scar tissue. This is scurvy, and a diet with no fruit or vegetables for months causes it.
options: Correct. Bleeding gums plus a wound that will not heal point to weak collagen: scurvy.
A lack of vitamin K does cause bleeding, but it does not stop wounds from healing, and in adults it rarely comes from diet alone: it usually follows fat malabsorption or drugs such as warfarin.
Iron deficiency causes anemia and fatigue, not bleeding gums and failed wound healing.
B12 lack causes anemia with large red blood cells and nerve damage, and it takes years to appear because the liver stores so much.

why.correct: The fat-soluble vitamins are A, D, E and K. Vitamin C and the B vitamins, including folate, are water-soluble.
options: Correct. Vitamin A is fat-soluble.
Vitamin C is water-soluble; it is stored little and needs a steady supply.
Correct. Vitamin D is fat-soluble.
Folate is a B vitamin (B9), and the B vitamins are water-soluble.
Correct. Vitamin E is fat-soluble.
Correct. Vitamin K is fat-soluble.

why.correct: Bile is needed to absorb fat, and the fat-soluble vitamins travel with fat. Blocking the bile duct lets fat pass into the feces and cuts absorption of A, D, E and K. The first sign in the blood is often slow clotting, because vitamin K stores are the smallest. Water-soluble vitamins are absorbed normally.

variables.name: Fat in the feces
variables.why: Without bile salts, fats are poorly emulsified and cannot form micelles, so much of the dietary fat passes through unabsorbed.

variables.name: Absorption of vitamin K
variables.why: Vitamin K dissolves in fat and enters the absorptive cells in micelles; with no micelles, little is absorbed.

variables.name: Time for the blood to clot
variables.why: Without vitamin K, the liver cannot finish clotting factors II, VII, IX and X, so clotting slows.

variables.name: Absorption of vitamin C
variables.why: Vitamin C is water-soluble and is absorbed by carriers in the intestinal lining, which do not depend on bile.

why.correct: Vitamin A is fat-soluble. The extra is stored in the liver and fat tissue, so a large daily excess accumulates over months and can damage the liver and bones. Vitamin C is water-soluble; the body stores little of it and the extra leaves in urine.
options: Vitamin C is water-soluble, so the extra is excreted rather than building up, and it does not acidify the blood at these doses.
Correct. Fat-soluble vitamins accumulate; vitamin A toxicity is well documented.
Fat-soluble vitamins such as A are stored, not excreted, so the extra builds up.
Toxicity depends on whether the extra is stored. Water-soluble vitamin C is far less likely to accumulate than vitamin A.

why.correct: This is Wernicke encephalopathy from thiamine deficiency. Thiamine is the coenzyme for the enzyme that removes CO2 from pyruvate as it enters the mitochondrion. Brain cells rely on glucose broken down this way, so without thiamine they cannot make enough ATP. Heavy alcohol use cuts both intake and absorption of thiamine.
options: Vitamin A lack causes night blindness and a damaged cornea, not confusion and an unsteady walk.
Correct. Thiamine replaces the missing coenzyme and can reverse the eye signs within hours.
Vitamin C lack causes scurvy: bleeding gums and poor healing.
B12 lack also damages nerves, but it develops over years and causes numbness and anemia, not this sudden confusion with eye movement problems.

why.correct: An essential nutrient is one your body cannot make in enough amounts. Your liver makes glucose from amino acids, lactate and glycerol, so glucose is not essential, even though your brain uses a lot of it.
options: Lysine is one of the nine essential amino acids; your cells cannot build it.
Linoleic acid is an essential fatty acid; your cells cannot put a double bond near the tail end of the chain.
Iodine is a mineral, an element your body cannot make, and it is needed for thyroid hormones.
Correct. Your body can make glucose, so it does not have to come from food.

why.correct: Lysine is essential: her cells cannot make it. Rice supplies some lysine, but less than her cells need. A ribosome needs every amino acid in the sequence at the moment it adds it, so protein building slows to the pace the scarce lysine allows. Amino acids are not stored for later, so the unused ones are broken down for fuel. Adding beans, which are rich in lysine, covers the gap.
options: Cells cannot build lysine from other amino acids; that is what makes it essential.
The sequence is set by the gene, so a ribosome does not substitute another amino acid for a missing one.
Correct. The scarce essential amino acid limits protein synthesis.
The body keeps no reserve of free amino acids set aside for later protein building.

why.correct: Thyroid hormones normally hold TSH release back by negative feedback. With less thyroid hormone, that brake weakens and the pituitary releases more TSH, not less. TSH is what makes the thyroid grow into a goiter.
options: This step is right. Iodine is needed to make thyroid hormones, and the thyroid gets it from the blood.
This step is right. Each thyroid hormone molecule carries three or four iodine atoms.
This step is right. Lower blood levels of thyroid hormone mean less reaches the pituitary.
This is the error. Less feedback means more TSH, which drives the gland's growth.
This step is right. Constant high TSH makes thyroid cells multiply and grow.

why.correct: Niacin is the vitamin part of NAD+. NAD+ accepts electrons in glycolysis and the citric acid cycle, becoming NADH, and hands them to the electron transport chain.
options: FAD is built from riboflavin (vitamin B2), not niacin.
Correct. Niacin forms part of NAD+.
ATP is the energy currency your cells make; no vitamin is needed as its building block.
Rhodopsin is the light-absorbing pigment of rods, built with vitamin A.

why.correct: Carbohydrate carbons already carry many oxygen atoms: they are partly oxidized. Fat is mostly carbon–hydrogen bonds, so each carbon has more electrons to give up as it is oxidized to CO2, and more energy is released per gram.
options: Both are absorbed almost completely in healthy people; the difference is in the molecules, not absorption.
Correct. Fat is less oxidized to start with, so it releases more energy as it is fully oxidized.
The number of enzymes does not set how much energy a molecule holds; the chemistry of its bonds does.
Storage with little water makes stored fat tissue denser in energy than glycogen, but it does not change the energy in a gram of pure fat.

why.correct: Iron from plants is absorbed poorly. Vitamin C eaten at the same meal keeps it in the form the intestine takes up best, so absorption rises several-fold.
options: Substances in tea bind plant iron and reduce its absorption.
Calcium taken at the same time reduces iron absorption rather than raising it.
Correct. Vitamin C with the meal improves absorption of iron from plant foods.
Vitamin E is an antioxidant for membranes and does not help iron absorption.

why.correct: Folate carries one-carbon groups needed to make DNA bases, and the embryo's cells are dividing fast. The neural tube closes about four weeks after the pregnancy begins, often before the pregnancy is known, so folate must already be adequate. Low folate at that time raises the risk of neural tube defects.
options: Myelin forms much later in development, and it is B12, not folate, that keeps myelin healthy.
Correct. Rapid cell division needs folate, and the neural tube closes very early.
Folic acid is advised to prevent neural tube defects, not nausea.
Folate is water-soluble and stored little, so it cannot be banked for months ahead.

why.correct: B vitamins supply no energy; they are parts of coenzymes. Once a well-fed person has enough coenzyme, the enzymes of fuel breakdown are not limited by it, so extra vitamin does not release more energy. The extra water-soluble vitamin leaves in her urine.
options: Vitamins are not fuel. A vitamin tablet supplies 0 kcal.
Fuel breakdown is not limited by coenzyme supply in a well-fed person, so adding more does not speed it.
Correct. Extra B vitamins do not add energy when stores are already adequate.
B vitamins are coenzymes for fuel breakdown, including fat breakdown, not blockers of it.

why.correct: Zinc is a cofactor for hundreds of enzymes, including those that copy DNA and build proteins. A lack slows growth, wound healing and immune cells, and dulls taste.
options: Iodine lack causes goiter and hypothyroidism; it does not explain poor taste or slow wound healing.
Fluoride lack raises tooth decay but does not cause this pattern.
Sodium is a major mineral, not a trace mineral, and a lack of it does not cause this picture.
Correct. Slow growth, poor healing, infections and loss of taste together point to zinc.

why.correct: Minerals are grouped by the amount needed. Trace minerals, such as iron, zinc and iodine, are needed at less than 100 mg a day; major minerals, such as calcium and sodium, at more.
options: Correct. The dividing line is the amount needed each day.
Many trace minerals come from plants: zinc from legumes and seeds, for example.
Iron is stored in the liver, but iodine is concentrated in the thyroid; storage site is not the definition.
Trace minerals act as ions dissolved in body fluids or bound to proteins.

why.correct: Vitamin C keeps the iron in the collagen-strengthening enzymes working. Without it, collagen cannot be stabilized, and as the body replaces old collagen with weak collagen, vessel walls and gums lose strength until they bleed.
Retinal, made from vitamin A, is the light-absorbing part of rhodopsin in rods. Rods run short of rhodopsin first when vitamin A is low, so vision in dim light fails before anything else.
options: Vitamin D becomes calcitriol and raises calcium absorption; it is not part of any visual pigment.
Vitamin E is an antioxidant that protects membrane lipids.
Correct. Vitamin A supplies retinal.
Vitamin B12 is needed for DNA synthesis and myelin, not for visual pigments.

why.correct: A food-label Calorie is a kilocalorie, and sugar supplies about 4 kcal per gram. Grams = 120 ÷ 4 = 30 g.
options: Correct. 120 kcal ÷ 4 kcal per gram = 30 g.
13 g divides by 9, the value for fat. Sugar is carbohydrate, at about 4 kcal per gram.
480 multiplies instead of dividing. Grams are kilocalories divided by kilocalories per gram.
120 treats each gram as 1 kcal. Carbohydrate supplies about 4 kcal per gram.

why.correct: Glucose enters most cells by facilitated diffusion, down its concentration gradient. Hexokinase converts it at once to charged glucose-6-phosphate, which the carriers do not carry out. Free glucose inside stays low, so the gradient into the cell is kept.
options: Correct. Trapping glucose as glucose-6-phosphate keeps the inward gradient.
This step spends ATP rather than making it, and entry through glucose carriers is facilitated diffusion, not pumping.
Hexokinase acts inside the cell; it does not change the number of carriers. Insulin does that in muscle and fat.
Adding a charged phosphate makes the molecule less able to cross lipid, not more.

why.correct: Phosphofructokinase, which commits the sugar to glycolysis, is inhibited by high ATP (and by citrate) and activated by AMP. When ATP is plentiful, glycolysis slows; when ATP is spent and AMP rises, it speeds up.
options: High ATP signals that the cell needs no more; it slows glycolysis rather than speeding it.
Glycolysis is tightly regulated, mainly at phosphofructokinase.
Correct. ATP inhibits phosphofructokinase, the main control point.
A resting, well-fed muscle has glucose available; the slowdown comes from the ATP signal, not a lack of glucose.

why.correct: In the middle panel, each three-carbon piece gives two electrons to NAD+, making one NADH, and the energy released adds a free phosphate. With two pieces per glucose, 2 NADH are made.
options: The first panel is the energy-consuming phase, where 2 ATP add phosphates to glucose; no NADH is made there.
Correct. Each of the two three-carbon pieces makes one NADH in the middle panel.
The last panel makes 4 ATP, not NADH.
One NADH is made per three-carbon piece, and there are two pieces, so 2 in all.

why.correct: Each turn of the cycle releases 2 CO2, and one glucose gives two acetyl CoA, so the cycle releases 4. The other 2 are released as each pyruvate becomes acetyl CoA. All 6 carbons of glucose leave as CO2.
options: 2 is the release per turn. One glucose drives two turns.
This misses the 2 CO2 released when the two pyruvate become acetyl CoA, before the cycle.
The cycle releases 4; the other 2 come from the pyruvate step, outside the cycle.
Correct. 4 from two turns of the cycle, plus 2 from pyruvate breakdown.

why.correct: Glucose is split in the cytosol; each pyruvate becomes acetyl CoA in the matrix; the citric acid cycle finishes oxidizing the carbon and loads the carriers; the carriers feed the electron transport chain; and the H+ gradient it builds drives ATP synthase.

Blocking complex IV stops electron flow and oxygen use. No H+ is pumped, the gradient collapses and oxidative phosphorylation stops. Cells fall back on glycolysis and lactate production, and unused oxygen stays in venous blood.

variables.name: Oxygen used by the cells
variables.why: Complex IV is where oxygen accepts electrons; with it blocked, oxygen is no longer taken up.

variables.name: H+ gradient across the inner mitochondrial membrane
variables.why: Electrons stop flowing, so the complexes stop pumping H+, and the gradient runs down through ATP synthase and small leaks.

variables.name: ATP made by ATP synthase
variables.why: With no gradient to drive it, ATP synthase stops making ATP.

variables.name: Lactate released into the blood
variables.why: Falling ATP speeds glycolysis, and pyruvate is turned into lactate to regenerate NAD+.

variables.name: Oxygen left in venous blood
variables.why: Oxygen is still delivered but the tissues cannot use it, so more of it stays in the blood returning to the heart.

why.correct: Cyanide from burning plastics blocks complex IV. Oxygen reaches the tissues but cannot accept electrons, so it stays in the venous blood, which looks red. Without oxidative phosphorylation, cells rely on glycolysis and turn pyruvate into lactate.
options: Her saturation of 99% shows oxygen is loading normally in the lungs.
That could explain high lactate, but not venous blood full of oxygen: working muscle takes more oxygen out, not less.
Mature red blood cells never have mitochondria; that is normal and does not explain these findings.
Correct. A block at the end of the chain explains high venous oxygen and high lactate together.

why.correct: 3 NADH × 2.5 = 7.5; 1 FADH2 × 1.5 = 1.5; plus 1 ATP made directly. 7.5 + 1.5 + 1 = 10 ATP per turn, or 20 per glucose.
options: 5 counts only the carriers (3 + 1 + 1) as if each were worth one ATP.
9 leaves out the ATP made directly in the cycle.
12 uses the older whole-number values (3 × 3 + 2 + 1). Current values are 2.5 and 1.5.

why.correct: Only 2 of the stage's 20 ATP are made directly. The other 18 come from the 6 NADH and 2 FADH2 the cycle makes, whose electrons drive the electron transport chain and ATP synthase.
options: The direct part is the short segment, 2 ATP per glucose.
The cycle runs in the mitochondrial matrix, and pyruvate breakdown has its own bar.
The bars show ATP made, not ATP spent.
Correct. Most of the bar is credit for the loaded carriers the cycle hands to the chain.

why.correct: NADH gives its electrons to complex I, which pumps H+. FADH2 gives its electrons to complex II, which pumps none, so they pass through only complexes III and IV. They pump about 6 H+ instead of about 10, which makes about 1.5 ATP instead of 2.5.
options: FADH2 carries two electrons, like NADH.
The FADH2 of the citric acid cycle is made by an enzyme in the inner membrane itself, not in the cytosol.
Correct. Entering after complex I means fewer H+ are pumped.
Its electrons do pass through complexes III and IV; they skip only complex I.

why.correct: The complexes pump H+ out of the matrix into the intermembrane space. That builds a high H+ concentration outside the inner membrane, so H+ can then flow back into the matrix through ATP synthase.
options: This step is right. Complex I accepts electrons from NADH.
This step is right. Each transfer releases a little energy.
This is the error. The pumps move H+ out of the matrix, not into it.
This step is right. Oxygen is the terminal electron acceptor.
This step is right. The returning H+ drives ATP synthase.

why.correct: Glycogen breakdown gives glucose-1-phosphate, which becomes glucose-6-phosphate. Only liver and kidney cells have glucose-6-phosphatase to remove the phosphate. In muscle, glucose-6-phosphate stays trapped and goes into glycolysis in that muscle.
options: Muscle breaks glycogen down whenever it works, day or night; the question is where the glucose goes.
Muscle has plenty of glycogen phosphorylase; that is how it uses its own glycogen during exercise.
Between meals insulin is low, and the block is an enzyme that muscle lacks, not a hormone.
Correct. Without glucose-6-phosphatase, muscle keeps its glucose for itself.

why.correct: Phosphorolysis adds phosphate across each bond, so each glucose leaves glycogen as glucose-1-phosphate and becomes glucose-6-phosphate without spending ATP. Glycolysis then nets 3 ATP from that glucose instead of 2.
options: Correct. The phosphate comes free from phosphorolysis, saving the ATP that hexokinase would spend.
Muscle cannot release glucose into the blood; the phosphorylated sugar stays in the cell.
Whether the sugar is oxidized with or without oxygen depends on the mitochondria and oxygen supply, not on how it left glycogen.
The gain is in ATP, not heat.

why.correct: Lactate and alanine become pyruvate, and glycerol enters as a three-carbon sugar phosphate; all three can be built into glucose. Fatty acids are broken down to acetyl CoA, and the step from pyruvate to acetyl CoA cannot run backward, so neither can become glucose.
options: Correct. Lactate is turned back into pyruvate.
Correct. Alanine, from muscle protein, becomes pyruvate once its nitrogen is removed.
Correct. Glycerol from stored fat enters as a three-carbon sugar phosphate.
Fatty acids are broken down to acetyl CoA, which cannot become pyruvate.
The step that makes acetyl CoA from pyruvate is one way only, so acetyl CoA cannot become glucose.

why.correct: Acetyl CoA joins oxaloacetate to make citrate, the six-carbon molecule that gives the citric acid cycle its name.
options: Correct. The first product is citrate.
Pyruvate is a three-carbon molecule made by glycolysis, before the cycle.
Glucose-6-phosphate is made in the first step of glycolysis, in the cytosol.
Succinate is a four-carbon molecule made later in the cycle.

why.correct: At complex IV, each O2 accepts 4 electrons and 4 H+ and becomes 2 water molecules. Removing electrons from the end of the chain keeps them moving.
options: NAD+ accepts electrons earlier, from fuel molecules, and delivers them to the chain as NADH.
CO2 is a waste product of the citric acid cycle; it does not accept electrons from the chain.
Correct. Oxygen accepts the electrons at the end of the chain.
ATP synthase uses the H+ gradient; it does not accept electrons.

why.correct: Without glucose-6-phosphatase, the liver cannot release free glucose from either glycogen or gluconeogenesis. Blood glucose falls a few hours after each feed, glycogen piles up and enlarges the liver, and the trapped glucose-6-phosphate is pushed down glycolysis into lactate. This is glycogen storage disease type I.
options: Without glycogen synthase, glycogen could not be built, and the liver would not enlarge with stored glycogen.
The question says she makes glucose-6-phosphate normally, and the liver has its own form of hexokinase for glucose uptake.
She can break glycogen down to glucose-6-phosphate, so phosphorylase works.
Correct. The final step of glucose release is missing.

why.correct: Muscle gains 2 ATP from glycolysis of one glucose to 2 lactate. The liver spends 4 ATP and 2 GTP, 6 in all, to rebuild one glucose. Net: 2 − 6 = −4 ATP.
options: Correct. 2 gained − 6 spent = 4 ATP lost per turn.
The muscle gains 2, but the liver spends 6 rebuilding the glucose, so the loop as a whole costs energy.
6 is the liver's cost alone; the muscle's gain of 2 offsets part of it.
Rebuilding glucose costs more than glycolysis yields, so the loop cannot be free.

why.correct: Complexes I, III and IV pump H+ out of the matrix into the intermembrane space, drawn above the membrane with many H+. That high concentration drives H+ back through ATP synthase.
options: The pumps remove H+ from the matrix, so its H+ concentration is lower.
H+ is charged and does not collect in the lipid core of the membrane.
Correct. The pumped H+ gathers in the intermembrane space.
The channel is only a path for H+ to flow down its gradient; it does not store H+.

why.correct: With ATP synthase blocked, H+ cannot flow back into the matrix. The gradient grows until the pumps cannot push H+ against it, electrons stop moving, and oxygen use falls. The chain and ATP synthase are coupled through the gradient.
options: The chain can run only as fast as H+ returns to the matrix; blocking the return slows it.
The two are linked by the gradient, so blocking one slows the other.
Fuel is plentiful here; oxygen use falls because of the gradient, not because fuel runs out.
Correct. A gradient that cannot be spent stops the pumps, and electron flow to oxygen slows.

why.correct: 18 carbons give 9 acetyl CoA in 8 turns. Beta oxidation: 8 FADH2 × 1.5 = 12 and 8 NADH × 2.5 = 20. Citric acid cycle: 9 × 10 = 90. Total 12 + 20 + 90 = 122, minus 2 for activation = 120 ATP.
options: 90 counts only the acetyl CoA passing through the citric acid cycle, leaving out the NADH and FADH2 made by beta oxidation itself.
106 is the yield for 16-carbon palmitic acid. Stearic acid has one more turn and one more acetyl CoA.
122 forgets the 2 ATP spent activating the fatty acid.

why.correct: Each acetyl CoA holds 2 carbons, so 12 carbons give 6 acetyl CoA. Each turn cuts off one acetyl CoA, but the last turn splits a four-carbon piece into two, so only 5 turns are needed.
options: 6 acetyl CoA is right, but the last turn yields two acetyl CoA at once, so it takes 5 turns, not 6.
Each acetyl CoA carries 2 carbons, so 12 carbons make 6, not 12.
Correct. 12 ÷ 2 = 6 acetyl CoA, in 6 − 1 = 5 turns.
5 turns is right, but the final turn leaves two acetyl CoA, making 6 in all.

why.correct: Fatty acids do reach the brain, but its neurons carry out very little beta oxidation, so fatty acids supply only a small share of its energy. Ketone bodies are small and water-soluble, and the brain takes them up and burns them readily once blood levels rise.
options: Neurons have many mitochondria; they burn glucose and ketone bodies aerobically.
Fatty acids are not simply toxic to the brain; the limit is how little of them its neurons break down.
Ketone bodies are partly oxidized fatty acid products, so they hold less energy per gram than fatty acids, not more.
Correct. The brain burns little fatty acid, so the liver's ketone bodies stand in.

why.correct: Across the endocrine, metabolic and respiratory systems: no insulin means unchecked lipolysis and high glucagon, so the liver makes ketone bodies at its maximum rate. Their acid uses up bicarbonate and lowers pH, and the respiratory system responds with deep, fast breathing. Glucose is high at the same time because insulin-driven uptake has stopped.

variables.name: Lipolysis in adipose tissue
variables.why: Insulin normally holds lipolysis back; with none, and with glucagon high, fatty acids pour out of fat cells.

variables.name: Ketone bodies in the blood
variables.why: The liver's beta oxidation makes acetyl CoA faster than its citric acid cycle can use it, and it turns the excess into ketone bodies.

variables.name: Blood bicarbonate
variables.why: Ketone bodies release H+, and bicarbonate is used up buffering it.

variables.name: Blood pH
variables.why: Once buffering cannot keep up with the acid, pH falls below 7.35: ketoacidosis.

variables.name: Depth and rate of breathing
variables.why: Low blood pH stimulates chemoreceptors, which drive deep, rapid breathing that blows off CO2.

variables.name: Blood glucose
variables.why: Without insulin, muscle and fat take up little glucose, and the liver keeps releasing it.

why.correct: Some of the acetoacetate the liver makes loses CO2 on its own and becomes acetone. Acetone is volatile, so it leaves in the breath and gives the fruity, nail-polish smell.
options: Beta-hydroxybutyrate is the main ketone body in blood, but it is made by the liver, not muscle, and it is not volatile.
Ammonia has a sharp smell, but it is made into urea by the liver; the fruity smell here comes from a ketone body.
Correct. Acetone from acetoacetate leaves in the breath.
Glucose does not evaporate and has no smell; high glucose is lost in urine, not breath.

why.correct: The liver makes ketone bodies but lacks the enzyme needed to convert acetoacetate back to acetyl CoA. So it exports them, and heart, muscle, kidney and brain burn them instead.
options: Correct. Missing one enzyme makes the liver a producer, not a user.
Liver cells are packed with mitochondria; ketogenesis itself happens there.
The liver releases ketone bodies rather than taking them up, and its inability to burn them is about an enzyme, not uptake.
Ketone bodies are made when insulin is low; insulin is not what stops the liver using them.

why.correct: Both are making ketone bodies, the same acids. She still has insulin, which limits fat release, so ketone levels stay low enough for tissues to burn them and buffers to absorb their H+: ketosis. He has almost no insulin, so production runs far ahead of use and his pH falls: ketoacidosis.
options: Ketosis and ketoacidosis involve the same ketone bodies, all acids; the difference is how much is made.
Correct. Insulin is the brake that keeps ketosis from becoming ketoacidosis.
His kidneys are excreting large amounts of ketone bodies; the problem is production far above what can be cleared.
Her liver is making ketone bodies, which is why her level is raised at all.

why.correct: Epinephrine and norepinephrine switch lipolysis on quickly through beta receptor proteins and cyclic AMP; cortisol and growth hormone raise it more slowly. Insulin switches it off, even at low levels.
options: Correct. Epinephrine raises lipolysis within minutes, as in exercise or stress.
Insulin blocks lipolysis; it is the main brake on fat release after a meal.
Correct. Cortisol helps release fatty acids and glycerol from fat.
Correct. Growth hormone makes fat cells break down stored fat.
Correct. Norepinephrine from sympathetic nerves acts on the same beta receptor proteins as epinephrine.

why.correct: Blocking HMG CoA reductase cuts cholesterol synthesis in liver cells. Short of cholesterol, the cells make more LDL receptor proteins, pull more LDL out of the blood by receptor-mediated endocytosis, and the blood level falls.
options: Correct. The liver makes up for lost synthesis by taking cholesterol from the blood.
Fewer LDL receptor proteins would leave more LDL in the blood, not less.
Statins act on an enzyme inside liver cells, not on LDL particles in the blood.
Statins block synthesis inside cells; they do not mainly change absorption from the gut.

why.correct: HDL (high-density lipoprotein) collects excess cholesterol from cells, including those in artery walls, and returns it to the liver.
options: Chylomicrons carry dietary triglycerides from the intestine.
VLDL carries triglycerides the liver has made out to muscle and adipose tissue.
LDL carries cholesterol out to body cells, not back to the liver.
Correct. HDL returns cholesterol to the liver.

why.correct: Lipoprotein lipase on capillary walls hydrolyzes the triglycerides in chylomicrons so the fatty acids can enter muscle and fat cells. Without it, chylomicrons full of triglyceride stay in the blood, and these large particles scatter light, making plasma milky.
options: Her plasma is milky because it is full of chylomicrons, so her intestine is making them.
A problem with LDL uptake raises cholesterol, but LDL particles are small and do not make plasma milky.
Lipolysis inside fat cells releases fatty acids bound to albumin, which do not make plasma milky.
Correct. Without the enzyme, chylomicrons cannot give up their triglycerides.

why.correct: Fat is released by lipolysis, carried on albumin, activated and carried into mitochondria on carnitine, cut into acetyl CoA by beta oxidation, and oxidized in the citric acid cycle; the carriers from both drive oxidative phosphorylation.

The amino group is first collected on glutamate by transamination, then released as ammonia by deamination in the liver. The urea cycle turns it into urea, which the blood carries to the kidneys for excretion.
ALT and AST are transaminases found in large amounts inside liver cells. When hepatitis damages those cells, the enzymes leak into the blood, so their blood levels track liver cell injury.
options: Correct. Injured liver cells release their contents, including these enzymes.
The rise reflects leakage from injured cells, not extra production.
Viruses use the host cell's machinery; they do not make transaminases.
The rise comes from the injured liver, not from reduced removal.

why.correct: The urea cycle runs in the liver, partly in its mitochondria and partly in its cytosol. The kidneys excrete the urea the liver makes; they do not make it.
options: This step is right. Transaminases pass amino groups to alpha-ketoglutarate, making glutamate.
This step is right. Deamination in liver mitochondria releases ammonia.
This is the error. The liver, not the kidneys, runs the urea cycle.
This step is right. One nitrogen comes from ammonia and one from aspartate.
This step is right. The kidneys excrete urea.

why.correct: The urea cycle is the liver's way of detoxifying ammonia. When it fails, ammonia rises and urea falls, and the brain suffers first.

variables.name: Ammonia in the blood
variables.why: Ammonia from amino acid breakdown and from gut bacteria is no longer turned into urea fast enough.

variables.name: Urea in the blood
variables.why: Less urea is being made, so less reaches the blood.

variables.name: Alertness and clear thinking
variables.why: Ammonia reaching the brain disturbs neurotransmission and swells astrocytes, causing confusion.

why.correct: A ketogenic amino acid's skeleton becomes acetyl CoA or acetoacetate. These can be burned, or made into ketone bodies or fat, but because acetyl CoA cannot become pyruvate, never into glucose.
options: Glucogenic amino acids give pyruvate; leucine's skeleton does not.
Urea carries the nitrogen, not the carbon skeleton.
Correct. Ketogenic skeletons end as acetyl CoA or ketone bodies.
Leucine not needed for protein is broken down; the body keeps no store of it.

why.correct: Glycerol enters gluconeogenesis as a three-carbon sugar phosphate. Fatty acids are broken down to acetyl CoA, which cannot become pyruvate, so they cannot be made into glucose.
options: Fatty acids end as acetyl CoA, which cannot be turned back into pyruvate or glucose.
Only glycerol can; fatty acids cannot.
Glycerol from stored fat is a real, if small, source of new glucose.
Correct. Glycerol is the only part of a triglyceride that can become glucose.

why.correct: The last step shown adds two hydrogens to acetoacetate's ketone group, turning it into beta-hydroxybutyrate, the main ketone body in the blood.
options: Correct. Beta-hydroxybutyrate is the reduced form of acetoacetate.
Acetone forms when acetoacetate loses CO2, not when it gains hydrogen, and it is not drawn in this figure.
HMG CoA comes before acetoacetate in the pathway, not after it.
Acetyl CoA is the starting material, at the far left.

why.correct: Deamination removes the amino group from glutamate as ammonia, in liver mitochondria.
options: Correct. Deamination releases the amino group as ammonia.
Lipolysis splits triglycerides, not amino acids.
Beta oxidation breaks down fatty acids.
Lipogenesis builds fatty acids and triglycerides.

why.correct: High insulin after carbohydrate meals switches on the enzyme that makes malonyl CoA from acetyl CoA, the committed step of lipogenesis. Glucose carbon passes through acetyl CoA and citrate into new fatty acids, which the liver packs into VLDL for storage in adipose tissue.
options: Glucagon is low when carbohydrate is plentiful, and beta oxidation breaks fat down rather than building it.
Lipolysis releases stored fat; it does not build new fat.
Ketogenesis runs when insulin is low and fat breakdown is fast, not when carbohydrate is plentiful.
Correct. Insulin drives lipogenesis.

why.correct: In the absorptive state, insulin is high and glucagon low. The liver takes up glucose, switches on glycogenesis, and switches off glycogenolysis. It stops releasing glucose into the blood; the little gluconeogenesis that continues feeds glycogen.
options: Glycogenolysis is switched off after a meal; the liver is storing glucose, not releasing it.
Insulin stops the liver releasing new glucose into the blood; any glucose it still makes goes into glycogen.
Correct. The fed liver stores glucose as glycogen.
Ketogenesis runs when insulin is low and fat breakdown is fast, not after a carbohydrate meal.

why.correct: After an overnight fast, the liver releases glucose from glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis, roughly half from each.
options: Muscle cannot release glucose into the blood, because it lacks glucose-6-phosphatase.
Absorption of a meal is over within about four hours.
Fatty acids cannot be made into glucose, because acetyl CoA cannot become pyruvate.
Correct. The liver supplies the blood's glucose between meals.

why.correct: A week without food drives insulin down and lipolysis up across the endocrine system and adipose tissue. The liver's glycogen is gone, and it makes ketone bodies from fatty acids. The brain, the nervous system's heaviest glucose user, switches partly to ketone bodies, lowering its glucose need and sparing muscle protein.

variables.name: Insulin in the blood
variables.why: Without food, glucose stays at the low end of normal and beta cells release little insulin.

variables.name: Lipolysis in adipose tissue
variables.why: Low insulin removes the brake on lipolysis, and growth hormone, cortisol and sympathetic activity push it further.

variables.name: Ketone bodies in the blood
variables.why: The liver turns the flood of fatty acids into ketone bodies, whose level climbs over the first week.

variables.name: Liver glycogen
variables.why: Liver glycogen is used up within about a day; after a week almost none is left.

variables.name: Glucose used by the brain each day
variables.why: The brain takes up ketone bodies in proportion to their level, so it needs less glucose.

why.correct: At day 14, glucose supplies about 40% of the brain's energy, and ketone bodies supply the rest, about 60%.
options: About 10% is the ketone share near day 2, before levels have risen.
About 40% is glucose's share at day 14, not the ketone bodies' share.
Correct. The dashed ketone line is near 60% at day 14.
Ketone bodies never supply that much in the graph; glucose still supplies about a third even at day 28.

why.correct: Early in a fast, most new glucose is made from amino acids. As ketone bodies rise, the brain takes more of its energy from them, so less glucose, and therefore less protein, is needed.
options: Correct. The two panels move together: more ketone use, less protein broken down.
Most muscle protein is still there at day 28; breakdown falls because less is needed.
Insulin stays low throughout a fast; that is what keeps lipolysis and ketogenesis high.
Fatty acids cannot be made into glucose; they are made into ketone bodies instead.

why.correct: Glucagon, epinephrine and cortisol break down stores and raise blood glucose, opposing insulin. Insulin and IGF-1 build and store.
options: Insulin is the main anabolic hormone: it drives uptake and storage.
Correct. Glucagon releases glucose from the liver.
Correct. Epinephrine drives glycogenolysis and lipolysis.
Correct. Cortisol breaks down muscle protein and drives gluconeogenesis.
IGF-1, made in response to growth hormone, builds protein and tissue: it is anabolic.

why.correct: Glucose between meals comes only from the liver's glycogen and gluconeogenesis. When muscle and most other tissues burn fat instead, that glucose is left for the brain and red blood cells, which depend on it. This is glucose sparing.
options: Muscle keeps its glycogen for itself; it cannot release glucose into the blood.
Correct. Glucose sparing protects the brain's supply.
Insulin is low between meals, and burning fat does not raise it.
Fatty acids cannot be made into glucose.

why.correct: After a few days, ketone bodies made by the liver from fatty acids rise high enough that the brain takes them up and burns them. This cut her brain's glucose need, and the smaller amount of glucose it still needed came from gluconeogenesis, mostly from amino acids.
options: Muscle glycogen cannot leave the muscle as glucose, and it is small compared with 12 days of need.
Fatty acids cannot become glucose; only the glycerol from fat can.
The brain burns little fatty acid; its neurons carry out very little beta oxidation.
Correct. Ketone bodies stand in for much of the brain's glucose.

why.correct: Without insulin, the signal of plenty is missing. His liver keeps releasing glucose, muscle and fat take little up, lipolysis runs unchecked and the liver makes ketone bodies. His body acts as if it were fasting, even with glucose far above normal.
options: Correct. Hormonally, he is in an extreme fasting state.
Storage in the absorptive state depends on insulin, which he lacks.
With no insulin, glucagon is not restrained, and the liver keeps adding glucose to already high blood levels.
Without insulin, the liver also releases glucose rather than storing it.

why.correct: First the meal supplies glucose. Between meals the liver breaks down its glycogen. Once glycogen runs out, within about a day, gluconeogenesis from amino acids takes over. After several days, rising ketone bodies cut the brain's glucose need, sparing protein.
After a carbohydrate meal, glucagon release falls. Rising glucose and insulin damp the alpha cells. High insulin with low glucagon is what defines the absorptive state.
options: This step is right. The portal vein carries absorbed glucose and amino acids to the liver first.
This step is right. Rising glucose drives insulin release.
This is the error. Glucagon falls after a carbohydrate meal.
This step is right. Insulin moves GLUT4 to the membrane, and muscle stores glycogen.
This step is right. Insulin drives fat storage and blocks lipolysis.

why.correct: Insulin raises lipoprotein lipase in adipose tissue, which hydrolyzes the triglycerides in chylomicrons and VLDL so that the fatty acids can enter fat cells.
options: Glucose-6-phosphatase frees glucose from the liver; it has nothing to do with fat uptake.
Correct. Lipoprotein lipase unloads triglycerides from lipoproteins.
Glycogen phosphorylase breaks down glycogen, and it is switched off after a meal.
Hexokinase traps glucose inside cells; it does not act on chylomicrons.

why.correct: Cortisol breaks down muscle protein, releasing amino acids, and switches on gluconeogenesis in the liver. Its effects build over hours, which suits a fast lasting days.
options: Correct. Cortisol drives muscle protein breakdown and gluconeogenesis.
Insulin builds protein and is low during a fast.
Glucagon acts mainly on the liver, where it speeds gluconeogenesis, but it has little effect on muscle, which has almost no glucagon receptor proteins.
IGF-1 builds protein and tissue.

why.correct: Growth hormone is catabolic for fat, driving lipolysis so that tissues burn fat, and anabolic for protein, through IGF-1, which limits muscle breakdown. It also opposes insulin's effect on glucose, helping keep blood glucose up.
options: Growth hormone raises blood glucose rather than lowering it.
Growth hormone opposes insulin and releases fat rather than storing it.
By releasing fatty acids, growth hormone supports ketogenesis, and it reduces glucose use.
Correct. Fat out, protein kept: both help during a fast.

why.correct: With glycogen full and insulin high, the liver turns extra glucose into fatty acids by lipogenesis, builds triglycerides, and exports them in VLDL to adipose tissue for storage.
options: In the fed state the liver takes glucose up; it releases glucose when glucose is low.
Correct. Excess glucose becomes fat, exported in VLDL.
Ketogenesis is switched off when insulin is high.
Free glucose is not stored; it is trapped as glucose-6-phosphate and sent into glycogen or other pathways.

why.correct: Albumin, made by the liver, provides most of the colloid osmotic pressure that holds fluid in capillaries. With too little, fluid collects in the tissues: edema. This picture, called kwashiorkor, is linked to diets very low in protein, although other factors also seem to contribute.
options: The swelling is fluid, not fat; he is wasting elsewhere.
A child eating so little has low insulin, and the albumin finding explains the edema.
Correct. Low albumin lets fluid leave the blood and collect in the tissues.
A diet so low in protein cannot build muscle; his arms are thin.

why.correct: Mature red blood cells have no mitochondria, so they cannot burn fatty acids or ketone bodies. They make ATP by glycolysis alone, from blood glucose.
options: Skeletal muscle switches to fatty acids between meals.
Heart muscle burns mainly fatty acids, and ketone bodies too.
Correct. Without mitochondria, red blood cells rely on glucose.
The liver burns fatty acids between meals while it releases glucose for others.

why.correct: While fat lasts, it supplies most of the energy, and ketone bodies from it spare muscle protein. When fat runs out, protein breakdown rises and death follows. More fat means a longer protected phase.
options: Fat holds about 9 kcal per gram and muscle protein about 4, and losing protein is what kills.
Glycogen lasts only about a day and hardly affects survival over weeks.
Fat is the source of ketone bodies, not a block to them.
Correct. Survival depends mainly on how much fat a person starts with.

why.correct: Oxygen per day: 200 mL/min × 1,440 min/day = 288,000 mL = 288 L. Energy: 288 L × 4.8 kcal/L = 1,382 kcal/day.
options: Correct. 288 L × 4.8 kcal/L ≈ 1,380 kcal/day.
960 is 200 × 4.8, the kcal for 200 liters, not for a day's oxygen use.
1,730 kcal/day is the answer for 250 mL/min, not 200.
This is ten times too large: 288,000 mL is 288 L, not 2,880 L.

why.correct: BMI = weight ÷ height². 1.60 × 1.60 = 2.56; 70 ÷ 2.56 = 27.3 kg/m², which falls in the overweight range of 25 to 29.9.
options: 21.9 would need a weight of about 56 kg at this height.
43.8 divides by the height without squaring it (70 ÷ 1.60).
31.2 does not follow from these numbers; squaring 1.60 gives 2.56, and 70 ÷ 2.56 = 27.3.

why.correct: Surplus: 500 kcal × 28 days = 14,000 kcal. 14,000 ÷ 7,700 ≈ 1.8 kg. Over many more months, the gain would slow as his larger body spends more.
options: 0.5 kg is the gain from about one week, not four.
3.5 kg would need about 27,000 kcal of surplus, roughly twice this.
14 is the surplus in thousands of kilocalories, not kilograms.

why.correct: Across the nervous, integumentary and cardiovascular systems: the heat load raises skin blood flow and sweating, but humidity blocks evaporation, so core temperature climbs. Sweat losses and blood held in the skin cut venous return and stroke volume, and heart rate rises to compensate. This is the setting for heat exhaustion and heat stroke.

variables.name: Skin blood flow
variables.why: The hypothalamus drives more active vasodilation through sympathetic cholinergic nerves as core and skin temperature rise.

variables.name: Sweat rate
variables.why: The same nerves drive the sweat glands harder in response to the greater heat load.

variables.name: Share of her sweat that evaporates
variables.why: Humid air is close to saturated, so evaporation slows and much of the sweat drips off.

variables.name: Core temperature
variables.why: Air near skin temperature blocks radiation and convection, and humid air limits evaporation, so heat loss falls short of heat production.

variables.name: Stroke volume
variables.why: Sweat losses shrink plasma volume and more blood sits in the widened skin vessels, so less returns to fill the heart.

variables.name: Heart rate
variables.why: With a smaller stroke volume, heart rate rises to keep cardiac output up for both muscles and skin.

why.correct: In air hotter than skin, evaporation is the only route of heat loss. 870 ÷ 580 = 1.5 L per hour must evaporate, and more must be secreted if some drips off.
options: 0.7 L would remove only about 400 kcal.
1.0 L removes 580 kcal, less than the 870 kcal he makes.
5.0 L would remove about 2,900 kcal, far more than he makes.

why.correct: A core temperature above 40 °C with confusion is heat stroke. Damage depends on how long the core stays that hot, so the priority is rapid cooling, best by immersing him in cold water, before transport if that can be done safely.
options: His set point is normal; heat gain has outrun heat loss. Fever-reducing drugs lower a raised set point, so they do not help, and he cannot swallow safely while confused.
A blanket would trap heat and let his temperature keep rising.
Fluids and rest suit heat exhaustion, where the brain works normally. His confusion marks heat stroke, and he should not drink while confused.
Correct. Rapid cooling is the treatment for heat stroke.

why.correct: Heat stroke is defined by brain dysfunction with a very high core temperature. Confusion, odd behavior, seizures or coma point to heat stroke; in heat exhaustion the brain works normally.
options: People with exertional heat stroke are often still sweating, so sweaty skin does not rule it out.
A fast heart rate is common in both.
Correct. Brain dysfunction marks heat stroke.
Nausea is common in heat exhaustion and does not separate the two.

why.correct: Radiation, conduction and convection all move heat from warmer to cooler. When the surroundings are hotter than the skin, they add heat. Evaporation removes heat whatever the air temperature, as long as the air is not saturated.
options: Radiation now brings heat in from hotter surroundings.
Conduction adds heat from any surface hotter than the skin.
Moving air hotter than the skin adds heat by convection.
Correct. Evaporation of sweat is the only route left.

why.correct: With less fat, fat cells release less leptin, so the hypothalamus drives hunger and saves energy. Ghrelin from the stomach also tends to rise after weight loss. Both push toward regaining the lost weight.
options: Correct. Falling leptin and rising ghrelin both raise hunger.
High leptin and low ghrelin would both reduce hunger.
Higher insulin and leptin would signal plenty and reduce hunger.
Lower ghrelin would reduce hunger, not raise it.

why.correct: Stomach stretch, carried by the vagus nerve, and gut hormones released as food reaches the small intestine, such as cholecystokinin and GLP-1, act on the brainstem and hypothalamus to end a meal. Ghrelin and an empty stomach drive hunger.
options: Correct. Stretch-sensitive sensory receptors report a full stomach through the vagus nerve.
Ghrelin rises before meals and raises hunger.
Correct. Cholecystokinin is released as fat and protein reach the duodenum.
Correct. GLP-1 increases satiety; drugs that mimic it reduce appetite.
An empty stomach releases ghrelin, which makes you hungry.

why.correct: Norepinephrine from sympathetic nerves makes brown fat cells break down fat and open a channel protein in the inner mitochondrial membrane. H+ leaks back into the matrix without passing through ATP synthase, so the electron transport chain runs flat out and the energy is released as heat instead of ATP.
options: Brown fat does not contract; that is shivering, in skeletal muscle.
Fat stores chemical energy, not heat; heat must be made by oxidizing the fuel.
Brown fat's heat comes from oxidizing fuel in its many mitochondria, not from anaerobic glycolysis.
Correct. Uncoupling the H+ gradient from ATP synthesis turns fuel into heat.

why.correct: In the cold, sympathetic nerves release norepinephrine onto skin arterioles, narrowing them. Less warm blood reaches the surface, so the shell insulates the core.
options: This step is right. Skin sensors report the cold first, before the core cools.
This step is right. The preoptic area is the temperature control center.
This is the error. Skin arterioles narrow in the cold; they widen in the heat.
This step is right. Shivering raises heat production.
This step is right. Both effects oppose the fall in temperature: negative feedback.

why.correct: Stimulus, sensor, control center, efferent pathway, effectors, response. Because the response opposes the stimulus, this is negative feedback.

At a core temperature near or below 30 °C, the heart muscle is cold and electrically unstable. Jostling can trigger ventricular fibrillation. Rescuers keep him horizontal, handle him gently and rewarm him.
options: Shivering stops in moderate hypothermia because heat production fails, and it would help rather than harm.
Skin vessel tone is not the danger here.
Correct. A cold heart is prone to fatal rhythms.
Cold does not make bones brittle at these temperatures.

why.correct: Frostbitten tissue should be rewarmed rapidly in warm water, but only when it will not freeze again. Thawing damages small vessels, and refreezing thawed tissue causes far worse injury.
options: Correct. A thaw–refreeze cycle is worse than delaying rewarming.
Rapid rewarming in warm water is the treatment once refreezing is not a risk.
Warming a foot in warm water does not dangerously raise core temperature.
Sweating is not the concern in frostbite.

why.correct: In fever, pyrogens raise the hypothalamic set point, and fever-reducing drugs block the prostaglandins that do this. The runner has hyperthermia: her set point is normal, and heat gain has outrun heat loss. There is no raised set point for the drug to lower.
options: Sweat does not remove these drugs to any important degree.
These drugs lower fever in adults too.
The issue is not where the heat is made but whether the set point is raised.
Correct. Fever and hyperthermia differ at the set point.

why.correct: Thyroid hormones raise the number of sodium–potassium pumps and mitochondria in cells, so they use more ATP and oxygen. Her BMR rises, she spends more energy than she eats, and the extra energy is released as heat.
options: Correct. A raised BMR explains both weight loss and feeling hot.
Her hunger is rising in response to greater spending, which shows appetite regulation is working.
The weight loss comes from greater spending, not poor absorption.
Hyperthyroidism raises heat production; losing brown fat would lower it.

why.correct: Shivering is rapid, involuntary contraction of skeletal muscle. It does no outside work, so its energy becomes heat.
options: Sweating is a response to high temperature, by sweat glands.
Narrowing of skin vessels uses smooth muscle in the vessel walls, not skeletal muscle.
Correct. Shivering is done by skeletal muscle.
Flushing, from widened skin vessels, is a response to high temperature.

why.correct: BMI uses only weight and height. Muscle is dense and heavy, so a very muscular person can have a high BMI with little fat. BMI is a screen, not a measure of body fat.
options: His BMI is in the obesity range, but he has little body fat; BMI does not measure fat.
For him, BMI overestimates fat, not underestimates it.
Correct. BMI does not distinguish muscle from fat.
The numbers are consistent: 105 ÷ (1.80 × 1.80) = 32.4.

why.correct: Total energy use has three parts: the BMR, the energy used handling food (about 10%), and physical activity, the most variable part.
options: Correct. Physical activity is the third part.
Shivering is only one kind of muscle activity, and it happens mainly in the cold.
BMI is a ratio of weight to height, not a use of energy.
Radiation is a way heat leaves the body, not a separate use of energy.
